questions.q: What does validating an alert actually mean?
options: Automatically trusting the alert label if it sounds serious
Reading the alert's summary text more carefully a second time
Checking the raw data the alert is based on -- the actual log line or event -- to confirm the alert's claim is really true
Closing the alert without any further review
questions.explain: An alert's text is a summary written by whoever built the rule, not a verdict -- validation means checking the underlying raw data it's based on.

questions.q: What question does scoping answer that validation does not?
options: Which analyst is assigned to the alert
How far the activity reaches -- what other hosts, accounts, or systems might be touched by the same activity
What time zone the SIEM server is configured to use
Whether the alert's label was spelled correctly
questions.explain: Once something is validated as real, scoping shifts the question from what to do about this one alert to how far the activity has spread.

questions.q: In the worked example, what specific finding pushed the suspicious-login alert toward escalation?
options: The login came from a country the analyst had never heard of
The alert's severity field was set to "high" by the SIEM
No other finding mattered -- any new-location login escalates automatically
Scoping found the same account had accessed a file share it had never touched before, right after the login
questions.explain: The login alone looked containable at Tier 1; it was the unfamiliar file-share access found during scoping that changed the picture.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three real criteria for escalating an alert to Tier 2?
options: The activity is confirmed malicious and needs a response beyond what Tier 1 is authorized to take
The alert came in during a night shift
The analyst personally feels unsure, regardless of what the data shows
More than ten minutes passed since the alert fired
questions.explain: The three real criteria are confirmed malicious activity needing a broader response, unclear scope, or a need for deeper tools than Tier 1 has.

questions.q: If an alert is validated as malicious but is fully scoped and within Tier 1's authority to contain, what happens to it?
options: It must always be escalated to Tier 2 regardless of scope
It doesn't need to escalate -- it gets handled and documented at Tier 1
It is deleted from the queue without documentation
It is automatically reclassified as a false positive
questions.explain: Escalation is reserved for alerts that are confirmed malicious with unclear scope, or that need tools beyond Tier 1's -- not every validated true positive needs to go further.
